research_concepts: carryover effects after offensive play type
methodological_questions: Reliability of derived play-type classification from play-by-play
Sample size and sparsity for infrequent play types
Confounding by game state, lineup quality, and score differential
Appropriate possession-level PPP definition (handle end-of-quarter heaves, transition starts)
Multiple testing across many play types
Risk of regression-to-the-mean selection bias
Causal identification of carryover effect versus pre-existing differences
Threshold and statistical power for AVOID label decisions
own_inferences: The availability of multiple seasons and possession-level play-type records makes a broad correlational analysis feasible.
Causal interpretation of differences in opponent next-possession PPP will be severely limited without controlling for lineup quality, score, and time remaining.
Play-type sparsity will likely make inference unreliable for less common types, requiring either aggregation or exclusion.
AVOID labeling based solely on observed PPP differences risks overfitting to noise and ignoring confounding.
Own-sequence lags add a further layer of complexity and potential confound (e.g., past success may affect play-calling).
uncertainties: Exact size of opponent next-possession PPP differences for each play type under an adequately controlled model.
True false-positive rate when deciding AVOID labels after multiplicity adjustments.
Data quality of derived play-type fields, especially for ambiguous transition or broken-play sequences.
Whether own-sequence lags provide independent signal or merely reflect the same confounding structure as opponent carryover.
Stability of carryover effects across seasons and playoff versus regular-season settings.

historical_effect.explanation: No prior studies were retrieved; the decision relies entirely on methodological assessment of the question and data.

blocking_constraints.text: Many play types have insufficient sample sizes for reliable opponent next-possession PPP estimation.
Game state, lineup strength, and score differential are strong confounders of both play-type choice and next-possession outcomes.
Testing dozens of play types inflates false positives unless stringent multiplicity correction is applied, reducing power.
Plays called after sequences of unsuccessful possessions may show spurious next-possession improvement due to regression to the mean.
Play-type derivation from play-by-play may misclassify broken or transition plays, adding noise.

prior_work.summary: No historical studies were retrieved from the project's records relevant to this specific question.

risks.text: Infrequent play types (e.g., post-ups, hand-offs) may have fewer than 100 occurrences per season, leading to unstable PPP estimates and low power.
Without controlling for offensive/defensive lineup net rating, score differential, and game clock, any apparent carryover effect may be entirely spurious.
Evaluating many play types without pre-registration of hypothesis families and multiplicity correction will produce false AVOID labels.

If play type X is more frequently called after a poor offensive sequence, the next possession is likely to regress upward, creating a false signal of a beneficial carryover (or masking a harmful one).
The accuracy of derived play-type labels in the available graph database is unknown; misclassification dilutes effect sizes and introduces bias.
If AVOID labels are defined using future data (e.g., a season average PPP), using the same data to test the effect creates circularity. A strict temporal split is required.
The decision to label a play as AVOID based on the observed next-possession PPP needs a pre-specified, out-of-sample threshold to avoid overfitting.
If the baseline opponent next-possession PPP varies little across contexts, even a small raw difference could be statistically significant but practically meaningless.
Carryover effects may change across seasons or between regular season and playoffs, limiting the applicability of labels derived from historical data.

design.estimand: Conditional average opponent next-possession PPP (points per 100 possessions) for each offensive play type, adjusted for game state, lineup strength, and season, estimated separately for each play type versus a robust overall baseline.
design.unit: One offensive possession ending in a classified play type (excluding end-of-quarter heaves, clear garbage time, and possessions with missing defensive matchup data).
design.sample: NBA 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25 full regular seasons (pooled) for training; NBA 2025-26 regular season (post-May 2026 data) held out for validation. Exclude possessions where next possession is not clearly defined (quarter ends, overtime).
design.power: Calculated pre-registration: detect a ≥ 2.0 PPP difference (Cohen's d ~ 0.1) with 80% power at α = 0.05/30 (Bonferroni) requiring about 25,000 possessions per play type. Only play types with at least 5,000 observed possessions across the training sample will be evaluated; others aggregated into 'other' or excluded.
design.controls: Score differential (binned: -10+, -5 to -10, within 5, +5 to +10, +10+), period (1-4, OT), seconds remaining in period, offensive lineup net rating (rolling 10-game), defensive lineup net rating, home/away, result of preceding offensive possession (made/missed shot, turnover), clustered standard errors at team-season level.
design.falsification: 1) Placebo test: opponent PPP on the second next possession after the index play should show no systematic difference by play type under the null. 2) Random shuffling of play-type labels within possession windows to establish empirical null distribution. 3) Test that effect remains when restricting to possessions following made baskets to reduce RTM.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register the set of play types to test (max 25 common types). Use Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control at 0.05 across all play types. For AVOID label classification, require effect size ≥ +1.5 opponent PPP and FDR-adjusted p < 0.05, and confirm sign stability in the 2025-26 holdout season.
design.decision_rule: A play type is flagged for AVOID label if the adjusted 95% confidence interval for opponent next-possession PPP exceeds the league baseline by > 1.5 points per 100 possessions (a pre-registered practical threshold) and replicates in the holdout season with same direction and p < 0.10 (one-sided). No AVOID label assigned if the holdout fails or placebo tests are violated.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files frozen as of 2026-06-19 for training seasons; 2025-26 data version as of 2026-06-19 for validation. Play-type records from the project graph database built from these play-by-play sources, version tagged as of that date.

confounding in lagged possession analysis
sample size and sparsity for play types
data quality of play-type possessions
transition defense analytics after play type
risk of false positives in labeling plays as AVOID

You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

{"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["play-type labeling", "AVOID labels", "next-possession opponent PPP", "carryover effects", "own-sequence lags"], "methodological_questions": ["measurement reliability of opponent next-possession PPP", "confounding in lagged possession analysis", "sample size and sparsity for play types", "data quality of play-type possessions", "transition defense analytics after play type", "risk of false positives in labeling plays as AVOID"], "query": "opponent next-possession PPP after offensive play type and own-sequence lags as drivers for AVOID labels"}}

reasoning_details.text:
We need to parse the research question and the data description. The question: "Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter." This is about play-type labeling and data quality. Specifically, it asks whether the opponent's points per possession (PPP) on the next possession after the team runs a specific play type X is large enough to justify an "AVOID" label for that play type (presumably meaning it's a play type to avoid because it leads to poor defensive outcomes). Also, "own-sequence lags similarly matter" likely means that what the team does on its own next possession (or sequence of possessions) after running play X also matters (e.g., maybe the play type affects fatigue or floor balance, leading to worse offensive performance on subsequent possessions). So it's about evaluating the carry-over effects of play types on both offensive and defensive outcomes in subsequent possessions. The data includes play-by-play, substitution data, defensive matchups, derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points). It spans multiple seasons. So this is a question about whether the data can support labeling play types based on these lagged effects, potentially for a feedback loop to avoid certain plays.

The task is to decide whether the question can be answered with this data, what historical evidence exists, and assess methodological risks. First, stage 1: identify research concepts and methodological questions, then retrieve_history.

Research concepts: play type labeling, AVOID labels, next-possession opponent PPP after play X (defensive carryover), own-sequence lags (offensive carryover), data quality, derived play-type possession records. So concepts: "play type labeling", "AVOID labels", "carryover effects", "defensive transition", "offensive rhythm effects", "possession-level data", "lagged analysis".

Methodological questions: Can we reliably measure opponent next-possession PPP given that possessions might not be consecutive (e.g., substitutions, timeouts, end of quarter)? How are play types determined? Risk of measurement error, confounding (opponent quality, game context, score, rest), sample size (how many observations of each play type to detect meaningful differences?), multiple testing (many play types), leakage from future information if labeling? Also "AVOID labels" implies some threshold or decision rule. Historical evidence might include earlier studies on post-play defensive transition or shot quality after certain actions. The project likely has previously conducted studies on play-type labeling and data quality issues.

Thus, retrieve_history with:
research_concepts: ["play-type labeling", "AVOID labels", "next-possession opponent PPP", "carryover effects", "own-sequence lags"]
methodological_questions: ["measurement reliability of opponent next-possession PPP", "confounding in lagged possession analysis", "sample size and sparsity for play types", "data quality of play-type possessions", "transition defense analytics after play type", "risk of false positives in labeling plays as AVOID"]
query: "opponent next-possession PPP after offensive play type and own-sequence lags as drivers for AVOID labels"

Make the call.

Now we need to assess the research question: "Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter."

We have data: NBA seasons from 2022-23 through 2025-26 (complete and partial). Data includes play-by-play, substitution rotations, starters, defensive matchups, box-score summary, and derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database. So we have play-type labels (some derived), and we can compute next-possession opponent points per possession (PPP). The question is whether the opponent's next possession PPP after a particular play type X is large enough to be used to label that play as AVOID (i.e., avoid running it). Also, own-sequence lags (presumably, the team's own PPP on the next few possessions after running play X) similarly matter.

So essentially, the research question is about testing whether certain play types lead to systematic carryover effects on the next possession, for both the opponent (transition defense) and own offense (momentum/fatigue/regression). And whether these effects are large enough to justify labeling plays as AVOID.

Methodological issues:
- Measurement reliability of play-type labeling: derived play-type records may have errors.
- PPP on next possession: sample sizes for specific play types may be small, leading to noise.
- Causal inference: confounding because play type selection is not random; it's correlated with game situation (score, time, lineup), which affects opponent next-possession PPP.
- Look-ahead bias: if AVOID label is derived from future outcomes, but the research question might be about whether these effects exist to justify such labeling. But the phrasing "drive AVOID labels" suggests that if the effect is large enough, we would label that play as AVOID. So it's an exploratory question to see if there are meaningful differences.
- Risk of multiple testing if testing many play types.
- Small sample for rare play types, leading to unreliable estimates (EXPOSURE_SPARSITY).
- Measurement of opponent next-possession PPP: need to define a possession, handle end-of-quarter heaves, etc. (MEASURE_RELIABILITY).
- Potential for regression to the mean: if a play type is selected after a string of unsuccessful possessions, the next possession may differ due to mean reversion (RTM_SELECTION).
- Outcome-derived label: AVOID label is the outcome measure itself? If we define AVOID based on observed next-possession PPP, it's circular (OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL). But the question is whether that PPP is large enough to drive the labels, meaning we are evaluating whether the effect size warrants labeling. So the analysis would be: compute for each play type the average opponent next-possession PPP and compare across types. So label is not predetermined; it's the result. So no label error? But still, the concept of "AVOID labels" implies a binary classification based on thresholds. So maybe we'd need to set thresholds and test if they are significant. Multiple testing.

Now, testability: p_testable. With three full seasons (22-23, 23-24, 24-25) and partial 25-26, we likely have enough data for common play types. Play types are from derived records, so they exist. But we need to check sample sizes for each play type. The null hypothesis: no difference in opponent next-possession PPP across play types. Can we detect a meaningful difference? Power depends on effect size and sample size per play type. The question says "large enough" so we might require an effect size of say 0.05 PPP or something. With many play types, we might need large sample. I'd estimate p_testable moderate, say 0.7, because there are many play types, some rare, and confounding is strong. Blocking constraints: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER for rare plays, CONFOUNDING, MULTIPLE_TESTING, MEASURE_RELIABILITY of play type classification.

Risks: list multiple risk codes with explanations.

Predicted outcome: likely to be untestable for rare plays, but overall maybe inconclusive due to confounding, or artifact due to selection bias. I'd assign probabilities: supported 0.15 (maybe some play types do show significantly higher opponent PPP), rejected 0.15 (null overall), untestable 0.2 (if sample too small), artifact 0.3 (due to selection/confounding producing spurious effects), uncertain 0.2 (inconclusive). But these are rough.

Decision: proceed_with_changes, specifying a more rigorous design: use causal inference methods, control for game state, restrict to common play types, pre-register thresholds and correction for multiple testing, etc. Or do_not_proceed if we think it's too flawed? I think it's worth proceeding with careful design, so proceed_with_changes.

Design: estimand: average difference in opponent next-possession PPP between play types, controlling for confounders. Unit: a possession. Sample: all possessions from the 3 full seasons, excluding garbage time, final seconds of quarters, etc. Power: likely high for frequent plays, low for rare ones. Controls: score margin, period, time remaining, offensive and defensive lineup strength (e.g., net rating), opponent, home/away, previous possession outcome, etc. Falsification: test that no effect exists on the second next possession (placebo test), or use randomization inference. Multiplicity: Bonferroni or false discovery rate adjustment for number of play types. Decision rule: declare AVOID label if adjusted p-value < 0.05 and effect size > some meaningful threshold, with robustness checks.

I'll output the JSON accordingly.
